systems.subsystemSummary: This is the boat itself: two sealed PVC pontoons for buoyancy and a flat PVC deck grid that only becomes rigid when steel cables, four turnbuckles, and a central compression mast snap it into a 3-D tetrahedron (a push-pull "tensegrity"). The pontoons float the load, the tensegrity deck carries the solar array, electronics box, and a 55-gallon reactor drum cradled low at the center of buoyancy. The whole subsystem's honest weakness is scale: two 6-inch tubes can't float a full drum, and the structure leans on furniture-grade plastic and (sometimes) rusting galvanized rigging — which is why the improved edition swaps in unsinkable dock floats and a bolted aluminum frame.

parts.label: J
parts.name: Pontoon tube
parts.realPart: 6 in PVC pipe (DWV/sewer wall, or Sch40), 10 ft, ×2 — e.g. Charlotte Pipe 6" PVC
parts.function: The two hulls — the primary flotation that keeps the raft and its payload on the surface.
parts.spec: 6 in dia × 10 ft, qty 2. Displaces ~300 lb of fresh water fully submerged (~150 lb usable at half-freeboard). Source conflict: build notes 6 in, BOM strings 14 in, polished docs 24 in — [VERIFY].
parts.howItWorks: A sealed air-and-foam column displaces water; buoyancy equals the weight of water it pushes aside (fresh water = 62.4 lb/ft³). The pair sets the entire payload budget.
parts.asBuilt: Two 10-ft × 6-in PVC pipes, one end capped, partially foam-filled, second cap seated with a sledgehammer.
parts.improved: Foam-cored HDPE dock floats sized to a 2× payload reserve (inherently unsinkable, UV-stable, no glued seam), or 12-in HDPE pipe filled solid with foam if keeping the round-tube look.
parts.cost: $80–250 for the pair (as-built PVC); $300–500 pair for dock floats
parts.source: AS-BUILT §3 + BOM #1; buoyancy math in §3 WARNING & Appendix A
parts.failureMode: A single end-cap seam leak floods the mostly-hollow tube; UV embrittles PVC; most fundamentally, 6-in tubes cannot float the ~460 lb full reactor drum.
parts.exploreNote: Two 6-inch tubes displace only ~300 lb submerged — but the reactor drum full of algae water is ~460 lb. The as-built literally cannot float its own payload full; you must run the drum part-empty or go bigger.

parts.label: I
parts.name: Pontoon end caps
parts.realPart: 6 in domed/rounded PVC caps, ×4 (2 per pontoon)
parts.function: Seal the pontoon ends into a watertight float — and the two forward caps double as the manatee's face.
parts.spec: 6 in, qty 4. One glued before foaming, one after.
parts.howItWorks: Solvent-welded to seal the air/foam column. One end is capped first; foam is poured down the open end; the second cap is glued and the whole tube inverted so gravity holds the wet cap seated while trapped-air pressure tries to blow it off.
parts.asBuilt: Primed + cemented, then the last inch driven home with a sledgehammer; notes omit primer (use it anyway).
parts.improved: Gasketed/fused caps on the pipe route; on the dock-float route the domed caps become purely cosmetic nose cones (foam) on the forward ends.
parts.source: AS-BUILT §3 Steps 3.3/3.6 + BOM #2; whimsy note in 00-GROUNDING
parts.failureMode: Sledge-seating crazes the socket and starts a leak; because the tube is mostly hollow, one leaking cap sinks that hull.
parts.exploreNote: The googly eyes go HERE — on the two forward caps, not on the drum. The round end caps are deliberately the manatee's face; that whimsy is the one design detail the grounding notes are emphatic about.

parts.name: Flotation foam
parts.realPart: 2-part, 2 lb-density pour polyurethane foam, ~2 gal kit — e.g. US Composites / Coast pour foam
parts.function: Reserve buoyancy — the unsinkable backup that keeps a hull afloat even if a cap leaks.
parts.spec: 2 lb/ft³ closed-cell; ~2 gal kit; staged 4–6 oz pours ×3 per pontoon.
parts.howItWorks: Mixing the two parts triggers an exothermic reaction that expands and cures into rigid closed-cell foam bonded to the pipe wall — displacement that stays even if the shell is breached.
parts.asBuilt: Staged pours 'until you can see foam' — which fills only a fraction of the ~2 ft³ pipe, leaving most of the tube hollow.
parts.improved: On the pipe route, fill the hull SOLID in ~5 staged lifts (control exotherm); on the dock-float route, foam is DELETED entirely (the floats are already foam-cored).
parts.cost: ~$60 per kit (as-built); $0 on the dock-float route
parts.source: AS-BUILT §3 Steps 3.5–3.6 + BOM #3; Appendix A foam-quantity note
parts.failureMode: Poured in one large batch it runs away thermally and expands violently; poured too sparingly (as built) it leaves the tube hollow so a cap leak still floods it.
parts.exploreNote: The build only fills a fraction of the pipe — so the foam gives you almost no real reserve buoyancy. For genuine unsinkability you fill the hull solid; the two-part kit is the same stuff used to float duck-hunting boats.

parts.label: C
parts.name: PVC deck frame pipe
parts.realPart: 1.5–2 in Sch40 PVC pipe, ~40–60 ft (furniture-grade or standard)
parts.function: The deck skeleton — ties the two pontoons together and carries the solar array, electronics box, and reactor drum.
parts.spec: 1.5–2 in dia, ~40–60 ft total, roughly a 5 ft square/rectangular perimeter — exact dims [MEASURE].
parts.howItWorks: Solvent-welded into a flat grid. Crucially it is NOT rigid on its own — it only stiffens once the tensegrity cables are tensioned against the mast.
parts.asBuilt: PVC perimeter built on multi-port fittings with pad-eyes at the corners for cable terminations.
parts.improved: Bolted 6061-T6 aluminum ladder frame (2×2 in × 0.125 in wall) — stiffer, ratable, bolts together, no creep; tensegrity kept only as an optional hardened aluminum+316-cable route.
parts.source: AS-BUILT §3 Step 3.7 + BOM #5; IMPROVED §5 change #2
parts.failureMode: PVC creeps (slowly deforms) under the sustained tensegrity preload and embrittles under UV — the tensegrity that stiffens the deck also slowly destroys it.
parts.exploreNote: PVC actually cold-flows under constant tension — so the very cables that make this deck rigid are also slowly stretching the plastic out of shape. It's fine for a demonstrator, wrong for a machine left out for months.

parts.label: H
parts.name: Frame fittings (4-way cross, tees, elbows)
parts.realPart: Multi-port 'four-way'/cross + tees + elbows, furniture-grade PVC — e.g. FORMUFIT 1.5", ×8–12
parts.function: Join the deck pipes into the frame grid and provide the corners where pad-eyes and cables anchor.
parts.spec: ~8–12 fittings; planar cross vs side-outlet 3-way geometry is undimensioned; furniture-grade, not structurally rated.
parts.howItWorks: Slip-fit and cemented; the corner elbows and center cross set the tetrahedron's geometry and locate every cable anchor point.
parts.asBuilt: Furniture-grade multi-port PVC fittings at corners and center.
parts.improved: Bolted aluminum joints (no plastic fittings) — or, on the hardened tensegrity route, cable pad-eye points welded/bolted to the aluminum.
parts.source: AS-BUILT §3 Step 3.7 + BOM #6; Appendix A '4-way fittings' note
parts.failureMode: Furniture-grade PVC is not load-rated — a cracked corner fitting collapses the whole tensioned deck.
parts.exploreNote: These are furniture-grade fittings — the kind sold to build PVC patio chairs and dog kennels — never rated for structural load. The rigidity of the entire raft rides on parts designed for lawn furniture.

parts.label: B
parts.name: Mast
parts.realPart: 2 in flared (bell-end) PVC, ~6 ft (as-built); 2 in 6061-T6 aluminum tube (improved)
parts.function: The sole compression strut — pushes down at the deck center so the upper cables can pull the corners up into a rigid 3-D tetrahedron; also carries the solar array and optional wind turbine.
parts.spec: Cut to ~5.5 ft (top-cap to bottom) + 6 in; 2 in dia.
parts.howItWorks: In a tensegrity, the mast is the lone compression member ('push') balanced against the cable network ('pull'). Preload is set by how far the turnbuckles are tightened against this strut.
parts.asBuilt: PVC cut 'by feel' to fit snugly between the pontoon end caps — loose means no preload; won't fit means trim a few inches.
parts.improved: Aluminum mast in a bolted base flange; on the recommended aluminum-frame route it is structural-only (carries the panel/turbine, no preload role — a low-mounted battery handles stability instead).
parts.source: AS-BUILT §3 Step 3.12 + BOM #7; IMPROVED §5 Step 5
parts.failureMode: A sloppy 'by feel' fit means no preload and a floppy deck; a PVC mast can buckle under full cable tension.
parts.exploreNote: The entire deck is stiff only because this one strut is jammed in compression — it's the 'push' in a push-pull tensegrity. Cut its length wrong by an inch and the whole raft goes floppy; there is no other structural backup.

parts.label: E
parts.name: Rigging cable
parts.realPart: 1/8 in 7×19 (or 7×7) aircraft cable, 316 stainless, ~50 ft
parts.function: The tension network — a lower flat 'X' plus upper corner-to-mast legs that snap the flat frame into a rigid tetrahedron.
parts.spec: 1/8 in, 316 SS; lower legs ~5 ft, upper ~6 ft. Sources waver 1/16–1/4 in; galv-vs-SS never stated — [VERIFY].
parts.howItWorks: Pre-tensioned cables carry pure tension while the mast carries compression; equal tension in all legs holds the geometry true. Slack anywhere and the tetrahedron collapses.
parts.asBuilt: Cut with a tape-wrap to stop fraying, formed into thimble eyes at each termination; grade unstated.
parts.improved: Standardize on 1/8 in 7×19 316 SS (corrosion-proof in a pond); dropped entirely on the bolted aluminum-frame route.
parts.source: AS-BUILT §3 Steps 3.8–3.11 + BOM #8; Appendix A cable-spec note
parts.failureMode: Galvanized cable rusts fast in water; a single failed leg drops the whole tensioned structure.
parts.exploreNote: It's literally aircraft control cable — the same 7×19 stranded wire that moves airplane flight surfaces — pressed into structural double-duty as the frame's tendons.

parts.label: G
parts.name: Wire rope thimbles
parts.realPart: 1/8 in wire-rope thimbles, 316 SS, ×8–12
parts.function: Protect each cable eye from crushing and chafe where it hooks a pad-eye or eyebolt.
parts.spec: 1/8 in, one per cable eye (8–12 total).
parts.howItWorks: The teardrop steel liner keeps the cable's bend radius open so the wire doesn't kink and fatigue at the anchor.
parts.asBuilt: A thimble eye formed at each termination, pried open to hook the center eyebolt.
parts.improved: 316 thimbles — or swageless mechanical terminals (Hayn Hi-Mod / Suncor) that eliminate thimbles and clips entirely for full-strength, tool-free eyes.
parts.source: AS-BUILT §3 Step 3.9 + BOM #9
parts.failureMode: Skip it and the cable bends too tightly at the anchor, fatigue-cracking at the eye under cyclic wave load.
parts.exploreNote: That little teardrop of steel is the difference between a cable eye that lasts years and one that quietly saws through itself at the bend — the cheapest part on the raft doing outsized work.

parts.name: Wire rope clips (saddle clamps)
parts.realPart: 1/8 in U-bolt wire-rope clips (saddle clamps), ×16–24
parts.function: Clamp each cable's tail back onto its standing part to form the load-bearing eye.
parts.spec: 1/8 in; minimum 2 per termination (so 16–24 for 8–12 eyes).
parts.howItWorks: The U-bolt and saddle pinch the two cable runs together; friction carries the load. The saddle must sit on the live/standing part, never the dead tail.
parts.asBuilt: First clamp ~5 in down with saddle on the standing end; a second clamp added above and ratcheted; re-torqued after first load.
parts.improved: Fully dimensioned: 3-1/4 in turnback, two 316 clips, ~3/4 in spacing, each nut to 4.5 ft-lb, re-torque after tensioning — or skip them entirely with swageless terminals.
parts.source: AS-BUILT §3 Steps 3.8–3.9 + BOM #10; IMPROVED §5 Step 6
parts.failureMode: 'Saddling a dead horse' (U-bolt on the live end) loses roughly half the termination's strength — the single most common rigging error.
parts.exploreNote: The rigger's rule 'never saddle a dead horse' is real and load-bearing: put the U-bolt on the wrong side of the cable and you throw away half your holding strength — a mistake invisible until the eye slips.

parts.label: F
parts.name: Turnbuckles
parts.realPart: 6 in hook-and-eye galvanized turnbuckle, ×4 (improved: 316 SS or hot-dip galv)
parts.function: The four upper-half tensioners — tightening them pulls the flat X and mast into a rigid tetrahedron and sets the preload.
parts.spec: 6 in; qty 4; net working cable ~4.5 ft after the body length.
parts.howItWorks: Opposite-hand threads at each end draw the two ends together as you turn the body, adding tension incrementally. You tighten them in opposing pairs to keep the mast centered.
parts.asBuilt: Hooked to the mast-top eyebolts, left fully extended for travel, then tightened evenly in opposing pairs a little at a time.
parts.improved: 316 SS turnbuckles on the hardened tensegrity route; DELETED entirely on the bolted aluminum-frame route.
parts.source: AS-BUILT §3 Steps 3.11 & 3.13 + BOM #11; IMPROVED §5 Step 6
parts.failureMode: Galvanized bodies rust and seize in water; uneven tightening warps the deck and off-centers the mast.
parts.exploreNote: These are the 'tuning pegs' of the whole structure — you tension the raft by turning them in opposing pairs, exactly the way you'd tune opposite lugs on a drum head to keep it flat.

parts.label: A
parts.name: Pad-eyes / eyebolts
parts.realPart: Galvanized or SS pad-eyes / eyebolts, ×8–12
parts.function: The hard anchor points every cable terminates on — frame corners, center, and mast top.
parts.spec: 8–12 total; galv or 316 SS.
parts.howItWorks: Bolted through the fittings/mast; the thimble eye hooks here, transferring cable tension into the frame and up to the mast head.
parts.asBuilt: Pad-eyes at the deck corners, eyebolts at the mast top and center junction.
parts.improved: 316 SS throughout; on the aluminum frame the corner eyes double as the 'LIFT ONLY HERE' hoist points.
parts.source: AS-BUILT §3 Step 3.7 + BOM #12; IMPROVED §5 Step 9
parts.failureMode: Galvanic corrosion at any mixed-metal anchor; pull-out from unrated furniture-grade PVC under load.
parts.exploreNote: Every cable's load funnels into these small anchors — and on the as-built they're bolted into furniture-grade plastic, making them the weakest link in the entire tension path.

parts.name: Drum cradle
parts.realPart: Saddle cradle + ratchet straps (as-built); bolted center-bay cradle (improved)
parts.function: Hold the 55-gallon reactor/settling drum centered and low at the center of buoyancy so it can't shift underway.
parts.spec: Sized to a 55-gal drum (~23 in dia × ~34 in tall); the drum is ~460 lb full.
parts.howItWorks: A saddle cradle plus straps lock the drum against roll and slosh; keeping it low and central keeps the raft's trim and lowers the center of gravity.
parts.asBuilt: Strap/cradle at deck center; handling rule is 'lift only from the pontoon corners, never the cables or panel.'
parts.improved: Bolted drum cradle in the aluminum center bay, with the battery mounted separately low as deliberate ballast.
parts.cost: ~$20–40 (straps/cradle; not separately line-itemed in the as-built BOM)
parts.source: AS-BUILT §3 Step 3.14 & §6 Step 6.5; IMPROVED §5 Step 8
parts.failureMode: A ~460 lb drum that shifts underway dominates trim and can capsize a beamy, lightly-loaded hull.
parts.exploreNote: The drum is by far the heaviest single thing on the raft — full, it outweighs everything else combined. This unglamorous cradle is all that stops ~460 lb of slurry from sliding and flipping the whole machine.

systems.subsystemSummary: This is the working guts of the Manatee: the loop that pulls algae-laden pond water in, screens it, concentrates it, slams it through a machined stainless micro-orifice nozzle to cavitate (lyse) the cells inside the 55-gallon drum, and pumps the recovered wax/oil off to storage. The heart is the Kinetic Nozzle — a triangular cluster of micro-bores that turns pump pressure into cavitation. Everything else exists to feed that nozzle clean slurry at the right pressure and to keep it from clogging, bursting a line, or eroding itself to death.

parts.label: FP1
parts.name: Intake coarse basket strainer
parts.realPart: T-H Marine / SeaSense bilge intake strainer or a clear-bowl raw-water Y-strainer (Groco ARG class) with a coarse basket — unknown exact model, needs id
parts.function: First-stage debris capture at the pond intake — keeps leaves, twigs, snails and stringy weed out of the loop before anything sensitive sees them.
parts.spec: 1/2-3/4 in hose barb; coarse basket ~1/8-1/4 in openings; polymer or bronze body. Exact size UNKNOWN [MEASURE to match intake hose].
parts.howItWorks: A slotted or basket screen sits in the suction line; water passes, solids stay in the basket, which you lift and empty. Purely passive.
parts.asBuilt: Called out as a mandatory coarse strainer on the intake in AS-BUILT §4.2 — the manual flags a missing strainer as 'the single most likely field failure.'
parts.improved: Kept as the coarse first stage, but now explicitly paired with a fine backflushable screen downstream (FP2) — coarse basket catches the big stuff so the fine screen lasts longer.
parts.source: West Marine / Amazon marine, off-the-shelf
parts.failureMode: Blinds over with algae mat and starves the intake pump (cavitation/overheat at the pump), or is left off and lets fiber reach the nozzle bores. Clean every run.
parts.exploreNote: This $20 basket is the cheapest part in the whole fluid loop and also the one whose absence most reliably kills the most expensive part — a clogged 0.014 in nozzle bore.

parts.label: FP2
parts.name: Backflushable fine mesh screen filter
parts.realPart: Rusco / Vu-Flow 1-1.5 in spin-down sediment filter, 100-150 mesh stainless screen, with flush valve + differential-pressure gauge
parts.function: Final clog defense right before the high-pressure pump — a mesh whose openings are smaller than the smallest nozzle bore, so nothing that gets through can lodge in the orifice.
parts.spec: 100-150 mesh (~100-150 µm opening); clear polymer bowl, 316 screen; ΔP gauge across it. Mesh MUST be finer than the smallest orifice bore (0.012-0.020 in ≈ 300-500 µm).
parts.howItWorks: Slurry spins through a cylindrical screen; particles collect on the inside and drop to a flush valve at the bottom. Open the valve to backflush without disassembly. Rising ΔP tells you it's loading up.
parts.asBuilt: Not present — the as-built rig had only the single coarse strainer, which is why micro-bore clogging is the top field failure.
parts.improved: NEW in the improved manual (change #6) — two-stage filtration with a ΔP gauge. The guiding rule: if the mesh opening is smaller than the smallest bore, nothing that passes can clog the nozzle.
parts.source: Irrigation / well-water supply (Rusco, Vu-Flow, Amiad)
parts.failureMode: Ignored ΔP creep → screen blinds → pump cavitates and loses feed pressure → no cavitation at the nozzle. Backflush on a schedule tied to the gauge.
parts.exploreNote: The whole two-stage filter philosophy is a size argument: pick a mesh finer than your smallest hole and clogging becomes geometrically impossible, not just unlikely.

parts.label: FP3
parts.name: Intake / transfer pump (bilge cartridge)
parts.realPart: Rule / Mayfair 12V bilge cartridge, 500-800 GPH (Rule-Mate / Attwood Tsunami T500 class)
parts.function: Low-pressure lift pump — draws pond water and surface algae up into the reactor drum. It moves volume, not pressure.
parts.spec: 12 VDC, 500-800 GPH nameplate (far less against head), ~2-4 A, 3/4 in outlet. Actual GPH UNKNOWN [MEASURE].
parts.howItWorks: A small centrifugal impeller in a snap-in cartridge flings water outward; cheap, self-cleaning of small debris, but produces only a few psi — it cannot and must not feed the nozzle.
parts.asBuilt: Photo-confirmed on the rig (Mayfair cartridge). AS-BUILT §4.2 mounts it to draw pond water + surface algae into the drum through the coarse strainer.
parts.improved: Unchanged in role and part — still a Rule/Mayfair 500-800 GPH cartridge for the low-pressure lift. Only the filtration downstream of it changed.
parts.source: Any marine/boat supply, off-the-shelf
parts.failureMode: Centrifugal impellers won't self-prime if mounted above water and can air-lock; nameplate GPH collapses against real lift head. Size to drum turnover, not the box number.
parts.exploreNote: It's a throwaway boat bilge pump doing intake duty — a nice example of the build's 'borrow a $30 marine part' logic instead of speccing a custom feed pump.

parts.label: FP4
parts.name: Circulation / immersion sump pump
parts.realPart: 12V vertical immersion sump/bilge pump — model unknown, role inferred (SEAFLO / Attwood submersible class), needs id
parts.function: In-drum recirculation / mixing on the as-built rig — kept the slurry moving and blended between nozzle passes.
parts.spec: 12 VDC vertical submersible; GPH and model UNKNOWN. Role itself is inferred from photos, not documented.
parts.howItWorks: A submersible impeller sits low in the drum and recirculates the batch so solids don't settle out of the flow path before they reach the nozzle feed.
parts.asBuilt: Present in the photo inventory as a third pump (bilge + immersion + diaphragm), role inferred as circulation. Undocumented function — flagged in grounding.
parts.improved: DELETED (BOM note, saves $40-90). The unloader-valve bypass return (FP9) plus the eductor (FP8) handle in-drum recirculation, so this redundant pump comes out entirely.
parts.source: Marine/pond supply, off-the-shelf
parts.failureMode: Runs dry if the drum level drops, and it's parasitic load on a 45 W budget. Its deletion is a case study in design-by-deletion — the bypass flow already does its job.
parts.exploreNote: This is the part the improved manual is proudest of removing: a whole pump whose function turned out to be a free byproduct of the pressure-relief bypass you needed anyway.

parts.label: FP5
parts.name: Cavitation pump (high-pressure feed)
parts.realPart: AS-BUILT: AR RMW2G24D pressure-washer pump. IMPROVED: small triplex plunger pump, AR RKA / Comet FDX class, on a 24-48V BLDC motor
parts.function: The muscle — pressurizes the concentrated slurry to a few hundred psi and drives it through the Kinetic Nozzle. This pressure is what creates cavitation.
parts.spec: As-built BOM caption '300 psi × 10 gpm 12VDC' (does NOT cleanly match the AR part — [VERIFY]). Improved target: ~1.5-2.5 gpm @ 250-400 psi, ~450-700 W on a 24-48V BLDC.
parts.howItWorks: A positive-displacement plunger/piston pump forces a fixed volume per stroke against whatever restriction the nozzle presents, building pressure. Cavitation intensity is set by throat velocity and downstream pressure — not by gpm — so you can cut flow ~5× while holding pressure and cut power ~5×.
parts.asBuilt: AS-BUILT §4.4 mounts the AR pressure-washer pump; the manual warns the '300 psi × 10 gpm' caption implies ~1.3 kW mechanical / ~2.5 kW electrical — far above the 45 W panel, so the machine can only batch-process at a tiny duty cycle.
parts.improved: The keystone change (#4). Right-sizing to low flow at adequate pressure cuts hydraulic power ~5×, shrinks the motor, extends runtime, and turns an impossible continuous claim into an honest solar-charged batch process.
parts.source: Pressure-washer pump supply (AR North America, Comet, General Pump)
parts.failureMode: Undersized pressure = no cavitation at all; oversized pump = blows the entire energy budget. Running dry or deadheading without an unloader destroys the plunger seals.
parts.exploreNote: The single most important physics insight in the whole build lives here: cavitation cares about velocity and back-pressure, not volume — so dropping the flow 5× barely touches the effect but slashes the power bill, which is the difference between 'can't run on solar' and 'can.'

parts.label: FP6
parts.name: Kinetic Nozzle (cavitation reactor)
parts.realPart: Custom CNC-turned + micro-drilled 316 stainless — NO off-the-shelf equivalent. Drawing title block says '306 S.S.' (a nonexistent grade — typo for 316). One-off from Xometry/Protolabs off the KineticNozzle1 drawings.
parts.function: The heart of the machine. Accelerates the pressurized slurry through a tight triangular cluster of micro-bores so local pressure drops below vapor pressure — cavitation bubbles nucleate and collapse, lysing algae cells and cracking a few percent of the organics per pass.
parts.spec: Triangular cluster: one central bore + three around it. Two drawn scales (4.20 in body and 0.3782 in body) are the SAME geometry scaled ~11.2×. Dimensioned spacings 0.16/0.25 in (large) and 0.01424/0.02225 in (small ≈ #79/#74 drill). Through-bore Ø and orifice length UNKNOWN — total orifice area, which sets both pressure and flow, is unknown. [MEASURE from the physical part]
parts.howItWorks: Bernoulli in the extreme: force fluid through a sub-millimeter throat and velocity spikes while static pressure collapses below the water's vapor pressure. Vapor cavities form, then implode microseconds later with enormous local pressure/temperature spikes that rupture cell walls (and erode the steel just downstream). The multi-jet cluster multiplies the cavitating zones.
parts.asBuilt: AS-BUILT §4.5 threads the 316 nozzle so it discharges into the drum below the liquid surface, oriented away from the wall (erosion) and the decant zone (re-mixing). Explicitly the one part you outsource to a machine shop, and explicitly a wear/consumable — order spares, use a quick-change fitting.
parts.improved: Becomes a 316L HOLDER carrying pressed carbide inserts (see FP7) — the erosion, cost, and unknown-bore problems solved at once. Body spec corrected to 316L throughout (change #5, #20).
parts.cost: $150-600 each (as-built, whole part is the consumable) / $100-200 holder (improved, insert is the consumable)
parts.source: One-off CNC: Xometry, Protolabs, or any precision machine shop from the dimensioned drawings
parts.failureMode: Two ways: (1) a single micro-bore clogs on grit/fiber and the jet pattern collapses — the top field failure, defended by FP1/FP2; (2) cavitation erosion pits the steel ~200 µm downstream of the bores until the orifice geometry (and thus the cavitation number) drifts out of spec. It literally eats itself; service life is UNKNOWN [MEASURE at commissioning].
parts.exploreNote: The two drawn nozzles aren't two designs — they're the identical part at 11.2× scale, which tells you the geometry is a deliberate ratio, not an arbitrary hole pattern. And the material callout '306 stainless' is a grade that has never existed — a title-block typo the whole corpus inherited.

parts.label: FP7
parts.name: Tungsten-carbide orifice insert
parts.realPart: Waterblast-grade tungsten-carbide orifice insert (StoneAge / Leland / Kennametal class), known bore 0.012-0.020 in, pressed into the 316L holder
parts.function: The improved-manual consumable — a hard, defined-bore jewel that does the actual orifice work so the expensive stainless body stops being the wear part.
parts.spec: Waterblast grade WC-Co carbide; bore 0.012-0.020 in class (known, not measured); 3-4 inserts in the triangular cluster + spares. Resists cavitation erosion ~10-50× vs 316.
parts.howItWorks: Same cavitation physics as the machined bore, but tungsten carbide's hardness shrugs off the implosion micro-jets that pit stainless. A pressed/known bore also fixes the orifice area, so pump pressure and flow become predictable instead of measured-after-the-fact.
parts.asBuilt: Does not exist in the as-built — the original micro-drilled 316 body was the whole consumable, at $150-600 a throw.
parts.improved: Change #5 — carbide inserts of known bore drop the consumable from a $150-600 whole-nozzle to a $15-40 insert, extend erosion life ~10-50×, and make orifice area a known quantity. The 'new razor-blade' of the machine.
parts.source: Waterjet/waterblast nozzle suppliers (StoneAge, Leland Ltd, Kennametal)
parts.failureMode: Press fit backs out or cracks under thermal/pressure cycling if the holder bore isn't right; a chipped carbide edge distorts the jet. Still borescope on the 24/72/168 h schedule.
parts.exploreNote: This one swap flips the economics: instead of scrapping a $150-600 machined part every erosion cycle, you press in a $20 carbide jewel — the same trick abrasive-waterjet cutters have used for decades.

parts.label: FP8
parts.name: Eductor / venturi injector
parts.realPart: Mazzei injector, 1078 or 1583 class (COTS stand-in for the custom 4-port part in the drawings)
parts.function: Concentration and mixing — entrains air/gas into the recirculation leg to float (dissolved-air-flotation style) and blend the algae toward the target solids so the nozzle feed is dense enough to be worth cavitating.
parts.spec: Polymer venturi injector; motive flow through a converging-diverging throat pulls suction on a side port. Sizing to slurry flow UNKNOWN [MEASURE]. A COTS Mazzei stands in for the custom 4-port part.
parts.howItWorks: Recirculated water speeds through the venturi throat, dropping pressure and sucking gas (or a second stream) in through the side port; the fine bubbles cling to algae and float it upward, concentrating solids at the surface where the intake draws densest slurry.
parts.asBuilt: AS-BUILT §4.3 plumbs the Mazzei-class injector into the recirculation leg to entrain gas and float/blend algae toward target solids, gated by a light/turbidity sensor. Concentration target is contradictory in sources (>6% vs ~30% solids — a ~5× disagreement) [VERIFY by moisture balance].
parts.improved: Kept, but fed from the unloader bypass (FP9) so it keeps mixing/floating while the HP pump idles between batches. Solids target resolved by moisture-balance measurement, since it sets the whole energy balance.
parts.source: Mazzei Injector Co. / irrigation & water-treatment supply
parts.failureMode: No moving parts, but the side port clogs and the throat scales; wrong sizing gives too little suction to float anything. The ~5× solids-target ambiguity is the real risk — guess wrong and every yield number is meaningless.
parts.exploreNote: It's a no-moving-parts dissolved-air-flotation trick borrowed from water treatment: a plastic venturi that concentrates the algae for free using nothing but the flow you already have.

parts.label: FP9
parts.name: Unloader / pressure-relief valve
parts.realPart: Pressure-washer unloader valve — AR ZK7-25, Comet VRT, or General Pump YU class
parts.function: High-pressure safety and anti-deadhead — caps line pressure below the hose rating and bypasses flow back to the drum if the nozzle blocks, and that bypass doubles as in-drum mixing.
parts.spec: Set below the 3000-psi hose rating (working range ~250-400 psi for the improved pump); bypass port routed back to the drum. Pressure-washer unloader, spring-and-piston type.
parts.howItWorks: A spring-loaded piston senses discharge pressure; when it exceeds setpoint (or the nozzle deadheads), the piston opens a bypass that dumps pump flow back to the tank instead of bursting the line. On a positive-displacement pump this is mandatory — the flow has to go somewhere.
parts.asBuilt: ABSENT — the as-built had no pressure relief. A blocked nozzle on a positive-displacement pump had nowhere to send its flow.
parts.improved: NEW (change #7). Set below hose rating, bypass to drum — prevents a blocked nozzle from bursting the line, and the bypass return does double duty as in-drum recirculation/mixing (which is what let the immersion pump FP4 be deleted).
parts.source: Pressure-washer parts supply (AR, Comet, General Pump)
parts.failureMode: Set too high and it protects nothing; set too low and it dumps to bypass before the nozzle ever cavitates. Piston seals wear and the setpoint drifts — check against the HP gauge.
parts.exploreNote: One cheap valve does three jobs at once: it's the burst-line safety, the anti-deadhead for the plunger pump, AND the recirculation mixer that made a whole separate pump unnecessary.

parts.label: FP10
parts.name: High-pressure hose, fittings & plumbing
parts.realPart: 3000-psi pressure-washer hose (3/8 in, M22/QC ends) for the nozzle-feed leg; low-pressure reinforced PVC hose, ball valves, check valves, tees, barbs for the rest
parts.function: The vascular system — carries slurry between drum, pumps, eductor, and nozzle. Only the nozzle-feed leg must be pressure-rated; everything else is low-pressure PVC.
parts.spec: Feed leg: 3000-psi rated pressure-washer hose. Low-pressure legs: 1 in reinforced PVC hose, ball valves for isolation, check valves for one-way flow. Line runs UNKNOWN [MEASURE the built layout].
parts.howItWorks: Positive-displacement pump discharge → HP-rated hose → nozzle; drum draws and returns run on ordinary reinforced hose. Ball valves isolate legs for service; check valves stop backflow into the wrong leg.
parts.asBuilt: AS-BUILT BOM #21 — 'the nozzle leg MUST be pressure-rated.' The low-pressure PVC legs, valves, and checks carry intake, return, and decant.
parts.improved: Same principle, spelled out: only the nozzle-feed leg is HP-rated; runs remain UNKNOWN and are measured on the built layout. Improved build adds the instrumentation tee (FP11) into the HP leg.
parts.source: Pressure-washer supply (HP hose) + hardware/irrigation (LP hose, valves)
parts.failureMode: Wrong hose on the feed leg is a burst-at-pressure hazard; a low-pressure diaphragm-pump line accidentally plumbed to the nozzle gets destroyed. Barbed clamps creep and weep at pressure — the feed leg wants proper HP threaded ends.
parts.exploreNote: The whole plumbing safety story is one rule: exactly one leg in the machine is high-pressure, and mixing it up with the low-pressure legs is how you either burst a line or destroy the transfer pump.

parts.label: FP11
parts.name: Inline instrumentation (flow/pressure/watt)
parts.realPart: Paddlewheel or turbine flow meter (GPI / Blue-White F-1000) + glycerin-filled HP pressure gauge (0-600 psi) + DC watt-meter (Bayite/Drok inline shunt)
parts.function: Turns every run into data — permanently measures true nozzle pressure and flow and the pump's watt-hours, so the yield/energy claims stop being assertions.
parts.spec: Flow meter sized to ~1.5-2.5 gpm; pressure gauge rated ≥500 psi (glycerin-filled for pulsation); DC watt-meter inline on the pump circuit. Read true P/Q off the gauges — never the BOM caption.
parts.howItWorks: A paddlewheel/turbine spins proportional to flow; a Bourdon gauge reads line pressure; a shunt-based watt-meter integrates volts×amps over time into watt-hours. Together they give the grams-oil-out ÷ watt-hours-in number the venture turns on.
parts.asBuilt: Not present on the HP leg — the as-built had only an LCD voltmeter, and metering was borrowed once at commissioning. AS-BUILT §7.5/7.6 has you add a gauge and log amperage only for the one commissioning run.
parts.improved: NEW permanent instrumentation (change #8). Inline flow meter + HP gauge + DC watt-meter make every run log Wh-in vs. grams-oil-out and read true nozzle P/Q directly — retiring the 'no power budget exists' flag.
parts.source: Process-instrument supply (GPI, Blue-White) + Amazon DC meters
parts.failureMode: Paddlewheel fouls in dirty slurry and under-reads; a non-glycerin gauge needle hammers itself to death on plunger-pump pulsation. Uncalibrated meters give confident wrong numbers — the worst kind.
parts.exploreNote: This is the cheapest part with the highest stakes: ~$100 of gauges is the entire difference between a venture that 'measures whether it works' and one that argues about it — the improved manual's central move.

parts.label: FP12
parts.name: Transfer / off-load diaphragm pump
parts.realPart: 12V diaphragm/RV pump — Shurflo 4008 or SEAFLO 33-series class, hydrocarbon-compatible (Santoprene/Viton) wetted parts
parts.function: Moves the recovered wax/oil — decants the floating layer to the bladder/jerricans and off-loads ashore. Transfer only; never the nozzle feed.
parts.spec: 12 VDC, ~45-55 psi, self-priming diaphragm pump; Santoprene/Viton wetted parts for the waxy lipid product. Shared part (decant + off-load).
parts.howItWorks: Flexing diaphragms with check valves self-prime and move viscous/semi-solid wax that a centrifugal pump can't — it pulls the thin floating layer over to storage without needing to be flooded first.
parts.asBuilt: AS-BUILT §4.7 — the diaphragm/RV pump handles decant/off-load into the bladder and 15-gal barrel. Explicitly 'keep the ~50-psi diaphragm pump strictly OFF the high-pressure loop — it cannot cavitate and will be damaged if plumbed to the nozzle.'
parts.improved: Unchanged in role; spec tightened to hydrocarbon-compatible Santoprene/Viton wetted parts and an inline suction strainer added to keep wax lumps out of the pump (change #19, §8 Step 7).
parts.source: RV/marine supply (Shurflo, SEAFLO)
parts.failureMode: Plumbed to the HP loop by mistake it's instantly destroyed; a plain-Buna diaphragm swells/degrades on the waxy hydrocarbon; semi-solid wax at low temp can stall it. It self-primes — but only if its check valves are clean.
parts.exploreNote: It's the exact opposite pump philosophy to the cavitation pump next to it — low pressure, self-priming, gentle — and the manual repeats three times that swapping the two is a great way to destroy a $60 part.

parts.label: K
parts.name: Wind turbine (optional)
parts.realPart: Southwest Windpower Air-X Marine 400 W 12 V (or dropped entirely)
parts.function: Optional secondary generation to top up charging on cloudy days or overnight when the panel is dark.
parts.spec: 400 W nameplate at 12 V, ~46 in rotor. Realistic pond average is tens of watts, not 400 W. NO rectifier / MPPT / dump-load exists in any schematic — an electrical gap.
parts.howItWorks: 3-blade permanent-magnet alternator; the Air-X has an internal regulator, but as wired on the raft there is no charge/diversion circuit tying it to the bus.
parts.asBuilt: Listed as an optional mast-top unit; never electrically integrated — no rectifier, MPPT, or dump-load in the corpus.
parts.improved: Dropped from the baseline (solar alone closes the trickle budget). If kept, a diversion/dump-load controller is mandatory — a turbine must never run unloaded.
parts.source: AS-BUILT BOM #23; IMPROVED change #15
parts.failureMode: Running unloaded with no dump-load overspeeds and cooks the alternator; mast-top mass raises the center of gravity and worsens capsize risk on a beamy hull.
parts.exploreNote: It looks like the main power source, but a 400 W turbine on a low-wind pond realistically averages tens of watts — and the 45 W solar panel is the only generation actually wired on the machine that was built.

parts.label: L
parts.name: Solar panel
parts.realPart: 45 W 12 V PV module (mono or amorphous), folding array
parts.function: Primary — and in practice the only — electrical generation on the built rig.
parts.spec: 45 W nameplate; ~17–21 V open-circuit; realistic ~120–170 Wh/day after real-world derating.
parts.howItWorks: PV cells produce DC above battery voltage; the charge controller regulates it down into the 12 V battery/bus.
parts.asBuilt: A 45 W folding panel — the sole generation source actually connected on the 2015 pond rig.
parts.improved: Same 45 W panel, but routed through an MPPT controller for +15–30% harvest from identical hardware.
parts.source: AS-BUILT BOM #22; IMPROVED BOM C
parts.failureMode: Algae film / soiling and shading from the drum or mast quietly cut output; a beamy raft can also let the panel sit at a poor sun angle.
parts.exploreNote: The machine's entire honest power budget rests on this one 45 W panel — about the output of a bright incandescent bulb — which is exactly why the cavitation loop can only run as a solar-charged batch process, never continuously.

parts.label: M
parts.name: Charge controller (PWM vs MPPT)
parts.realPart: As-built: generic 12 V PWM controller. Improved: Victron SmartSolar 75/15 MPPT
parts.function: Regulate panel output into the battery and prevent overcharge.
parts.spec: PWM: no maximum-power-point tracking, ~$15–30. MPPT: 75 V / 15 A, Bluetooth harvest log, programmable load output + low-voltage-disconnect, reverse-polarity protection.
parts.howItWorks: A PWM controller clamps the panel down to battery voltage (lossy — it throws away the panel's voltage headroom). An MPPT does a DC-DC conversion to hold the panel at its optimal voltage and harvest more power.
parts.asBuilt: Generic 12 V PWM, no MPPT.
parts.improved: Victron SmartSolar MPPT — adds harvest and doubles as the duty-cycle timer + LVD that replaces the trim-pot perfboard.
parts.source: AS-BUILT BOM #24; IMPROVED change #9
parts.failureMode: PWM wastes 15–30% of available energy on a budget that can't spare it; a bargain controller can also be damaged by reversed PV polarity.
parts.exploreNote: Swapping PWM for MPPT is free energy — 15–30% more from the same panel — and it throws in a programmable timer and low-voltage cutoff that make the hand-soldered controller board unnecessary.

parts.label: N
parts.name: 12 V deep-cycle battery
parts.realPart: Group 24/27 12 V AGM marine (improved: 12 V 50 Ah AGM or LiFePO4 w/ BMS)
parts.function: Overnight energy store and main 12 V bus source; buffers the gap between solar harvest and load.
parts.spec: Capacity never specified in the as-built corpus [MEASURE]. Improved baseline: 50 Ah for ~2 days autonomy at trickle-rig load.
parts.howItWorks: Sealed AGM lead-acid chemistry (~12.6 V full); charges from the controller, sources the bus through the distribution block.
parts.asBuilt: A Group 24/27 AGM marine battery; actual amp-hour rating undocumented.
parts.improved: 50 Ah AGM or LiFePO4, and mounted LOW between the hulls so it doubles as stability ballast.
parts.source: AS-BUILT BOM #26; IMPROVED change #3, BOM C
parts.failureMode: Deep discharge destroys AGM cycle life, and the as-built rig has no low-voltage-disconnect to prevent it.
parts.exploreNote: In the improved design the battery pulls double duty — dropped low between the hulls it becomes deliberate ballast that lowers the center of gravity, which is the single cheapest fix for the raft's untested capsize risk.

parts.label: O
parts.name: 2200 F supercapacitor
parts.realPart: 2200 F low-ESR ultracapacitor (series/balancing config undocumented)
parts.function: Buffer high-current inrush surges (e.g. pump start-up) that the battery handles poorly.
parts.spec: 2200 F; voltage/series config [MEASURE] — a 2.7 V cell needs ~6 in series plus balancing to make 12 V. The BOM separately lists a 3 F cap, an unreconciled contradiction.
parts.howItWorks: An electrostatic double-layer capacitor stores charge without chemistry — enormous capacitance at low voltage, able to source/sink brief high-current spikes.
parts.asBuilt: A 2200 F canister across the bus with no documented pre-charge resistor or cell-balancing.
parts.improved: Deleted from the baseline (the battery buffers the small pump); a factory-balanced 16 V module is added back only if a high-inrush motor pump is fitted.
parts.source: AS-BUILT BOM #25; IMPROVED change #10
parts.failureMode: A fully discharged 2200 F cap looks like a dead short and will arc-weld the terminals if connected directly; without balancing, series cells drift and one overvoltages.
parts.exploreNote: A drained 2200-farad cap behaves like a bolt laid across the battery — hook it up directly and it pulls hundreds of amps and welds the terminals; it has to be pre-charged through a resistor first.

parts.label: diode
parts.name: Blocking diode
parts.realPart: 50 A stud-mount rectifier diode
parts.function: Block reverse current so the battery doesn't back-feed and drain through the panel at night.
parts.spec: 50 A stud rectifier, installed in the PV positive lead, band toward the controller.
parts.howItWorks: A one-way valve for current — conducts panel-to-battery, blocks battery-to-panel.
parts.asBuilt: 50 A stud diode in the PV+ lead as reverse-block / battery isolation.
parts.improved: Deleted — the MPPT controller has built-in reverse-polarity protection, so the discrete diode is redundant.
parts.source: AS-BUILT BOM #32; IMPROVED change #9 (superseded)
parts.failureMode: Its ~0.7 V forward drop wastes power as heat on a tight budget; pointless once a proper controller blocks reverse current itself.
parts.exploreNote: This part exists only to patch a limitation of the cheap PWM controller — the moment you upgrade to MPPT, the diode becomes dead weight.

parts.label: P
parts.name: Bus bar / distribution block
parts.realPart: Dual 6-post marine bus bar (improved: Blue Sea ST-Blade fused block + negative bus)
parts.function: Central 12 V positive/negative distribution and single-point ground.
parts.spec: Dual 6-post as-built; improved 6-circuit fused distribution + separate negative bus bar.
parts.howItWorks: All module negatives bond to one negative bar (single-point ground to avoid ground loops); the positive bar is the switched 12 V distribution point.
parts.asBuilt: Dual 6-post marine bus bar — distribution only, no fusing.
parts.improved: Fused distribution block so every branch is individually protected.
parts.source: AS-BUILT BOM #27; IMPROVED change #12, BOM C
parts.failureMode: A loose lug becomes a hot resistive joint; with no fuses on the bar, any downstream short pulls straight from the battery.
parts.exploreNote: The as-built bus bar carries no fuses anywhere — a single chafed wire against the aluminum could dump the whole battery into a dead short.

parts.label: fuse
parts.name: Fusing (main + per-branch)
parts.realPart: Main terminal fuse (Blue Sea MRBF 60 A) + inline per-branch fuses
parts.function: Interrupt fault current before it starts a fire — the core life-safety element.
parts.spec: One main fuse on the battery positive post plus one fuse per load branch, each sized to the load, not the wire.
parts.howItWorks: A fusible link melts and opens the circuit when current exceeds its rating.
parts.asBuilt: NONE — there is no fusing anywhere on the built rig. Flagged 'add anyway.'
parts.improved: Mandatory MRBF terminal fuse on the battery post + a fused per-branch distribution block; do not energize without them.
parts.source: AS-BUILT BOM #41; IMPROVED change #12, Safety §2
parts.failureMode: Absence is the failure — a 12 V lead-acid (plus ultracap) bus can source hundreds of amps into a fault and start an electrical fire.
parts.exploreNote: This is the single cheapest life-safety part in the entire build — a few dollars of fuses — and it was completely missing from the machine that actually got built and floated.

parts.label: Q
parts.name: SSR relays (vs marine relays)
parts.realPart: 4× Fotek SSR-40 DD (40 A DC-DC) — improved: sealed 40 A automotive/marine relays or logic-level MOSFET modules
parts.function: Switch the 12 V loads (diaphragm pump, two air horns) from a logic-level control signal.
parts.spec: 40 A DC solid-state, polarity-sensitive, needs heatsinking. BOM says 6× SSR-100 DD while the as-built used 4× SSR-40 DD — unreconciled.
parts.howItWorks: An opto-isolated 3–32 VDC control input triggers an internal output transistor/MOSFET; DC SSRs are polarity-sensitive on both sides and dissipate heat while conducting.
parts.asBuilt: Four Fotek SSR-40 DD on a metal plate switching the pump and horns.
parts.improved: Sealed marine relays (near-zero voltage drop, no heatsink) or logic-level MOSFETs, each with a Schottky flyback diode.
parts.source: AS-BUILT BOM #28; IMPROVED change #11
parts.failureMode: Each SSR wastes ~5 W as heat at load and runs hot near its rating; wired reverse-polarity it simply won't switch.
parts.exploreNote: Each DC solid-state relay burns about 5 watts as heat while it conducts — trivial on shore power, but with four of them on a 45 W solar budget they can quietly eat a third of your generation.

parts.label: R
parts.name: LCD voltmeter
parts.realPart: 16×2 digital DC voltmeter module + calibration trim-pot
parts.function: Display bus voltage — the only instrumentation on the built rig.
parts.spec: 16×2 LCD, voltage only, no current sensing.
parts.howItWorks: Taps the bus positive/negative, reads voltage through an ADC, shows it on the display; trim-pot calibrates against a meter.
parts.asBuilt: The sole instrument aboard — voltage readout, nothing else.
parts.improved: Kept as a glance display, but paired with a coulomb-counting shunt that actually captures the power budget.
parts.source: AS-BUILT BOM #29; IMPROVED change #8
parts.failureMode: It shows voltage but hides current draw, so you cannot see whether the machine is gaining or losing energy over a run.
parts.exploreNote: Voltage alone can't tell you if you're winning the energy race — you need current, which is exactly the measurement this display omits and the whole venture's central claim depends on.

parts.label: shunt
parts.name: Battery monitor / shunt (improved add)
parts.realPart: Victron SmartShunt 500 A (or an INA226 module)
parts.function: Coulomb-count watt-hours in vs. out — the missing power-budget instrument.
parts.spec: 500 A precision shunt with Bluetooth logging; the INA226 alternative is ~$15.
parts.howItWorks: Measures the tiny voltage drop across a precision resistor in the battery negative path, derives current, and integrates it over time into watt-hours consumed vs. the MPPT's watt-hours harvested.
parts.asBuilt: Absent — the built rig had only the LCD voltmeter.
parts.improved: Permanently installed in the battery negative so all current passes through it; logs the daily energy balance every run.
parts.source: IMPROVED change #8, BOM C, Commissioning §9.4
parts.failureMode: n/a as-built (it was missing); if placed so a load bypasses it, the logged budget is wrong.
parts.exploreNote: This one part retires the venture's single biggest open question — it turns 'does the energy balance actually close?' from an argument into a number logged automatically on every run.

parts.label: S
parts.name: Perfboard controller
parts.realPart: Hand-soldered perfboard with a trim-pot threshold comparator
parts.function: The actual deployed 'processor' — switches the pump when a sensor/voltage crosses a set-point.
parts.spec: Discrete parts, single trim-pot set-point, ~$10. Not a computer, not AI.
parts.howItWorks: A comparator watches a light-sensor or bus voltage; when it crosses the trim-pot threshold it drives the SSR control input to turn the pump on/off.
parts.asBuilt: The real brain on the 2015 pond rig — not the BEAM board and not the MIT Cricket, both of which sat unused.
parts.improved: Replaced by the MPPT controller's programmable load output + low-voltage-disconnect.
parts.source: AS-BUILT BOM #30; IMPROVED change #14, §7
parts.failureMode: Floating logic inputs chatter the relay; a single trim-pot drifts with temperature; it logs nothing.
parts.exploreNote: The '3rd-generation Prospero AI inference engine' the marketing claimed was physically this — a hand-soldered perfboard with one trim-pot deciding when to turn the pump on.

parts.label: beam
parts.name: BEAM analog phototropism board (optional)
parts.realPart: 74HC14 'Nv' microcore + 74HC125 + photodiode bridge + discrete H-bridges (VBSXv2 / BasicJT2)
parts.function: Steer toward the brightest water — a cheap proxy for a surface algae bloom — using pure analog light-seeking.
parts.spec: 4.5 V rail; PD1/PD2 'Bright Sensor' bridge (2N3906/2N3904); 74HC14 microcore (0.1 µF + 3 M/10 M timing); 74HC125 reversing/halt gates; PN2907/PN2222/2N3906 H-bridges with 1N4148 flyback to FRONT/REAR thrusters.
parts.howItWorks: A Braitenberg/BEAM topology — imbalance between two photodiodes biases an analog 'Nv neuron' oscillator that pulses the H-bridges to turn the raft toward the brighter side. No microprocessor, no code.
parts.asBuilt: A design study only — no evidence it ever flew; the pond rig used the perfboard instead.
parts.improved: Chosen as the single steering path (the discontinued MIT Super Cricket is dropped); bench-verify on a scope that the microcore oscillates and the bridges reverse cleanly before water.
parts.source: AS-BUILT BOM #33; IMPROVED change #14, §7 Step 9
parts.failureMode: Built wrong, the microcore won't oscillate; H-bridge shoot-through can cook transistors; it is entirely unproven on water.
parts.exploreNote: This is honest 1980s BEAM robotics — a Braitenberg vehicle that steers toward light with about $20 of logic chips and photodiodes, no processor and absolutely no machine learning.

parts.label: sensors
parts.name: Light sensors
parts.realPart: Photodiodes / CdS photocells
parts.function: Sense the brightness differential that steers the raft (and can gate slurry turbidity).
parts.spec: 2 sensors for the BEAM bright-sensor bridge; 6 for the unused digital (Cricket) path.
parts.howItWorks: Two photodiodes form a bridge; an imbalance between them tells the controller which side is brighter, i.e. the steering direction.
parts.asBuilt: 2 for the BEAM path / 6 for the unused digital path.
parts.improved: A 2-photodiode bridge on the chosen BEAM path.
parts.source: AS-BUILT BOM #34
parts.failureMode: Biofilm or spray fouling blinds them; CdS cells respond slowly and drift with temperature.
parts.exploreNote: The robot's entire 'vision' is two photodiodes comparing which side is brighter — a fair proxy for a surface bloom, but it cannot distinguish algae from a bright water reflection or the sun's glare.

parts.label: horns
parts.name: Air-horn annunciators
parts.realPart: 2× 12 V marine air horns
parts.function: Purpose UNSTATED in the source corpus — likely a fault alarm or a bird/wildlife deterrent [VERIFY].
parts.spec: Two 12 V marine horns switched through SSR outputs.
parts.howItWorks: A 12 V diaphragm/compressor horn driven from a relay/SSR output.
parts.asBuilt: Two horns wired through the SSRs; their intended function is undocumented.
parts.improved: Kept, but confirm intent before wiring them always-armed; put each on its own fused branch with a flyback diode.
parts.source: AS-BUILT BOM #31; Appendix A
parts.failureMode: Inductive kickback without a flyback diode; unknown duty cycle could quietly drain the battery.
parts.exploreNote: Two marine air horns are wired into the machine and no one documented why — the leading guesses are a fault alarm or a deterrent to keep waterfowl from roosting on the raft.

parts.label: T
parts.name: Wiring & enclosure
parts.realPart: Marine tinned wire + ring terminals + heat-shrink; improved IP66 enclosure + marine glands + Gore breather + conformal coat
parts.function: Interconnect the electronics and protect them from a wet, floating environment.
parts.spec: Marine tinned wire as-built. Improved: IP66 box, MG Chemicals 422B conformal coat, marine cable glands, drip loops, breather vent.
parts.howItWorks: Tinned copper resists corrosion; a sealed box with a breather manages condensation; drip loops route water away from entries; conformal coat seals the boards.
parts.asBuilt: NO conformal coat, gasketed enclosure, or drip loops documented — an open box with a bare perfboard.
parts.improved: Full waterproofing package: IP66 enclosure mounted above the splash line, glands low, breather high, boards conformal-coated, drip loops on every entry.
parts.source: AS-BUILT §5.10, Appendix A; IMPROVED change #13, §7 Step 10
parts.failureMode: Water ingress — the number-one failure mode of a floating electronics box — causing corrosion and shorts.
parts.exploreNote: The built rig put a bare hand-soldered board in an open box on a raft — no conformal coat, no gasket, no drip loops — leaving water intrusion as the single most likely way the whole electronics package dies.

systems.subsystemSummary: The power chain is deliberately humble and that is its strength: a single 45 W solar panel (an optional 400 W turbine was specified but never properly wired) feeds a charge controller into a 12 V deep-cycle battery and a 2200 F supercapacitor on a common bus, from which rugged solid-state relays switch the pumps and air horns. The 'brain' the marketing sold as patented AI is really a hand-soldered perfboard with one trim-pot, with an analog BEAM light-seeker as the honest steering option — cheap, proven, un-exotic hardware. The real weaknesses are all sins of omission — no fusing, no waterproofing, no current metering — every one of which the improved edition adds so the machine can finally measure whether its energy balance closes.

This subsystem turns the raft's central 55-gallon drum into a combined cavitation reactor and gravity separator: cracked lipid/wax floats to the top, is skimmed off, buffered in a 15-gallon settling vessel, and pumped to soft/rigid final storage, while chlorophyll-laden water returns to the pond through a sub-surface tube. Separation is entirely passive — no heat, no distillation, just gravity, a weir, and (in the improved edition) a coalescing pack. The whole thing lives or dies on two elevations being right (skim port at the surface, S-return well below it) and on the free surface staying calm enough for a ~1/8-inch oil film to stratify on a moving raft, which is why the improved edition adds baffles, a stilling shroud, a self-leveling skimmer, and a sight glass.

parts.label: drum
parts.name: 55-gallon reactor / settling drum
parts.realPart: 55-gal open-head HDPE poly drum, bolt-ring gasketed lid (UV-stabilized/black on improved route). ~23 in dia x ~34 in tall. Vented, NOT pressure-rated.
parts.function: One vessel doing two jobs: it holds the recirculating slurry while the nozzle cavitates it, and it acts as the gravity separator where cracked lipid/wax floats and biomass sinks.
parts.spec: 55 US gal; ~23 in dia x ~34 in tall; HDPE; open-head with bolt-ring lid + gasket; lidded and vented, never sealed. Empty ~20-25 lb; full of water/algae ~460 lb.
parts.howItWorks: Fresh slurry is pumped in near the bottom; the high-pressure loop draws from low (heavy un-converted water) and re-injects the cavitated stream below the surface. Each pass releases a thin oily film that floats; injecting more slurry raises the level and displaces that film out the top decant. Gravity does all the separating — the drum is just a quiet, tall-enough tank.
parts.asBuilt: The 2024 model shows a plain central cylinder with no drawn internals; every port, tube, and weir below is inferred from process prose and older bench rigs. It is both reactor and separator, strapped low at the center of buoyancy between the pontoons.
parts.improved: Spec a UV-stabilized/black HDPE drum with a bolt-ring lid; add defined penetrations, internal anti-slosh baffles, a stilling shroud, a bottom sludge-drain valve, and a gooseneck vent. Function unchanged.
parts.source: Uline / grainger / drum supply houses; any food-grade or industrial 55-gal HDPE open-head drum.
parts.failureMode: Run full on 6-in pontoons and it swamps the raft (a full drum is ~460 lb vs ~150 lb usable buoyancy). Second failure: a moving raft sloshes the surface and re-mixes the oil film so nothing separates. HDPE also creeps/embrittles under sustained UV over a long deployment.
parts.exploreNote: This single cheap poly drum is simultaneously the reactor, the settling tank, and the biggest single stability liability on the whole boat — a full one outweighs everything else on deck combined.

parts.label: penetrations
parts.name: Drum penetration fittings
parts.realPart: Uniseal grommets or threaded PVC bulkhead fittings, 1-2 in; 4-6 as-built, 6-8 on improved route.
parts.function: Leak-tight pipe pass-throughs cut into the drum wall for every fluid line: nozzle return, biomass feed, S-return, skim/decant, sight-tube, and vent.
parts.spec: 1-2 in Uniseal or threaded bulkhead; count/size/elevation UNKNOWN in the corpus — [MEASURE] on your unit. Improved route: 6-8 penetrations including sight-tube (2 fittings) and vent.
parts.howItWorks: A Uniseal is a rubber grommet that seals on a plain drilled hole as the pipe compresses it; a threaded bulkhead clamps with a gasket and backing nut. Port elevation is the whole game — the skim port must sit right at the top liquid line, the S-return inlet well below it.
parts.asBuilt: Four penetrations inferred: nozzle recirculation return, fresh-biomass feed, sub-surface S-tube outlet, and a top decant/overflow port at the max liquid line. Elevations never drawn.
parts.improved: Six-plus defined penetrations, and the added clear sight-tube lets you set and verify port elevations empirically instead of guessing before you drill.
parts.source: Uniseal (uniseal.com / Amazon); Banjo/Spears threaded PVC bulkheads at irrigation suppliers.
parts.failureMode: Get the two key elevations wrong and separation fails entirely — a decant port too low skims water, an S-return too high siphons off your product oil. A feed-port leak is a high-pressure hazard; a decant leak silently loses product.
parts.exploreNote: Nobody ever dimensioned where these holes go — and the entire separation function hinges on two of them being at exactly the right height, which is why the improved build adds a sight glass to dial them in by eye.

parts.label: weir
parts.name: Decant weir port → floating weir skimmer
parts.realPart: As-built: PVC tee + standpipe/weir fitting at the top liquid line. Improved: off-the-shelf self-leveling floating weir surface-skimmer head.
parts.function: The take-off point that pulls only the floating oil/wax layer off the top of the drum and sends it to storage.
parts.spec: As-built weir/standpipe: ~$10-20. Improved floating skimmer head: $30-60, self-leveling intake that rides the surface. Layer skimmed is thin — reference jar shows ~1/8 in oil over ~3-5/8 in green liquid.
parts.howItWorks: As-built: a fixed weir lip at the max liquid line — rising level from fresh slurry pushes the top film over the lip (displacement decanting, not pumping). Improved: a floating head whose intake self-levels exactly at the surface film regardless of level or raft motion, feeding the transfer-pump suction.
parts.asBuilt: Fixed weir standpipe/tee at the top port, hand-timed. Builder is told to make it valved so oil release can be controlled vs. just recirculating. Give the oil time to stratify before decanting.
parts.improved: Replace the fixed lip with a self-leveling floating weir skimmer sitting inside a stilling shroud — a ~1/8-in film can't reliably decant over a fixed knife-edge on a raft that pitches and rolls.
parts.source: Pond/aquarium surface skimmers, oil-spill weir-skimmer heads, or a shop-built floating box weir.
parts.failureMode: Fixed weir on a moving raft: wave-induced sloshing continuously carries water over the lip, so you decant mostly water. Floating skimmer: float can jam against the shroud wall if clearances are tight.
parts.exploreNote: The floating oil layer it has to catch is only about an eighth of an inch thick — thinner than a pencil — which is exactly why a fixed lip fails and a self-leveling float is worth the upgrade.

parts.label: s-tube
parts.name: Sub-surface "S" return tube
parts.realPart: ~1 in Sch-40 PVC with two 90-degree elbows forming an S/gooseneck; inlet mouth sits below the oil layer.
parts.function: Returns clarified, chlorophyll-laden water from the drum back toward the pond/growth side, drawing from below the floating product so it doesn't steal oil.
parts.spec: ~1 in Sch-40 PVC + 2 elbows; inlet elevation must be clearly sub-surface (below the oil layer), drawn from the clarified mid-low zone. Improved route feeds it off a screened low sidewall bulkhead valve.
parts.howItWorks: The S-bend places the intake mouth at a controlled depth below the surface film. Water leaving the system is pulled from this clarified zone, so the light oil/wax stays behind to be skimmed. It's the 'clean water out' path — the subsystem's honest lead deliverable.
parts.asBuilt: Assembled from ~1 in Sch-40 PVC and two 90-degree elbows so the inlet sits below the expected oil layer; connected to the S-return bulkhead. Warned: too high and it siphons off your product oil instead of water.
parts.improved: Take it off a low sidewall bulkhead ball valve with a screened intake in the clarified mid-low zone; the valve doubles as a cleanout, and the added sight glass confirms the inlet is safely below the interface.
parts.source: Any PVC/irrigation supplier — standard Sch-40 pipe and elbows.
parts.failureMode: Set the inlet too high and it siphons off the product oil you just worked to release; too aggressive a draw pulls the interface down and re-entrains oil into the return.
parts.exploreNote: This humble bent pipe is the part that actually delivers the machine's honest headline benefit — cleaner water back to the pond — while everything upstream chases the wax bonus.

parts.label: baffle
parts.name: Anti-slosh baffle + skimmer stilling shroud
parts.realPart: HDPE baffle plate(s) or slotted center tube + a short open-top HDPE cylinder/sleeve around the skimmer. Improved-edition addition; absent in as-built.
parts.function: Damps bulk sloshing inside the drum and gives the floating skimmer a locally calm pool so gravity separation survives a raft that pitches and rolls.
parts.spec: 1-2 HDPE baffle plates (or slotted center tube) + a stilling shroud sleeve around the skim zone; must NOT fully partition the drum (loop must still circulate) and must stay removable/perforated near the bottom for cleanout.
parts.howItWorks: Baffles break up the standing wave that raft motion sets up in a 55-gal free surface. The stilling shroud is a mini-tank-within-the-tank: it isolates a small pool at the surface where the skimmer sits, so even while the drum surface heaves, the skim pool stays flat enough for the ~1/8-in film to hold.
parts.asBuilt: None. The as-built has a bare open free surface — gravity separation on a moving raft with nothing to calm it. Flagged in Appendix A as an unresolved sloshing problem.
parts.improved: Add baffles + shroud, and gate skimming to calm/moored windows if motion still carries water. This is one of the two 'fragile assumption' fixes the improved edition is built around.
parts.source: Cut from HDPE sheet / a smaller poly bucket; shop-fabricated, no special part.
parts.failureMode: Over-baffle and you block the recirculation loop; under-baffle and the surface never stills, so no separation happens underway. Media/plates foul with biomass and need periodic removal.
parts.exploreNote: It's the cheapest fix for the deepest flaw: gravity separation needs a still pond, but this thing lives on a boat — so you build a tiny still pond inside the tank.

parts.label: coalescer
parts.name: Coalescer / settler media pack
parts.realPart: Corrugated-plate (oil-water separator) pack or coalescing media, installed inside the 15-gal settling vessel. Improved-edition addition; absent in as-built.
parts.function: Passively breaks the oil-in-water emulsion that cavitation can throw — merges fine dispersed oil droplets into a decantable layer with no heat or power.
parts.spec: Corrugated OWS plates / coalescing media; sized to the 15-gal vessel; must be removable for cleaning. Passive, zero added power draw. Paired with flat-black exterior + mild passive solar warming to cut wax viscosity.
parts.howItWorks: Slurry that has been violently cavitated arrives as a stable oil-in-water emulsion — tiny oil droplets that won't float on their own. As it creeps through the closely-spaced corrugated plates, droplets collide with the plate surfaces and each other, coalesce into larger drops, and rise. Warm (flat-black, sun-heated) wax is less viscous and separates faster.
parts.asBuilt: None. The as-built has no de-emulsification step at all; Appendix A flags emulsion stability as an unmeasured risk that could defeat the whole gravity-separation premise.
parts.improved: A defined clear-sided coalescer/settler with a corrugated-plate pack + passive solar warming — 'breaks it with no heat/power,' the elegant part of the improved separation train.
parts.source: Coalescing/OWS plate media from separator suppliers, or DIY corrugated HDPE/PP sheet stacks.
parts.failureMode: Media fouls with biomass and channels if not cleaned; if cavitation makes an emulsion too stable, even coalescing plates may need mild heat — an unproven step until the commissioning run measures it.
parts.exploreNote: Cavitation is so violent it can emulsify the very oil you're trying to recover — this passive plate pack quietly un-does that damage using nothing but geometry and sunlight.

parts.label: barrel15
parts.name: 15-gallon settling / coalescer barrel
parts.realPart: 15-gal HDPE poly drum; ~14.5 in dia x ~27 in tall. Improved route: clear-sided, flat-black exterior, houses the coalescing pack.
parts.function: Intermediate buffer between the drum's skimmer and final storage — lets the skimmed oil/wax settle and coalesce before it's committed to the storage tank.
parts.spec: ~15 gal; ~14.5 in dia x ~27 in tall; HDPE. As-built role 'ambiguous' [VERIFY]. Improved: defined as a passive coalescer + settler with bottom water-drain routed back to the S-return and a top take-off for coalesced product.
parts.howItWorks: Skimmed product (still carrying some water) lands here and sits. Free water drops out the bottom drain back to the S-return; coalesced oil/wax rises and is taken off the top to final storage. On the improved route it holds the coalescing media and is warmed passively by flat-black paint in sun.
parts.asBuilt: Present but its role is genuinely unclear in the source corpus — treated as a settling/holding buffer, flagged [VERIFY]. Plumbed drum decant -> (barrel) -> bladder.
parts.improved: Given a real job: a clear-sided coalescer/settler with defined bottom-drain and top take-off, flat-black for passive warming, media removable for cleaning.
parts.source: Any 15-gal HDPE drum supplier; clear/translucent versions for the interface-watching improved route.
parts.failureMode: As-built, its purpose is undefined enough that a builder may plumb it as dead volume that does nothing. Passive solar warming, if overdone, can soften/stress the HDPE.
parts.exploreNote: In the original build nobody could say for sure what this barrel was even for — the improved edition rescued it by turning the mystery buffer into the emulsion-breaking coalescer.

parts.label: sight
parts.name: Sight glass / level & interface gauge
parts.realPart: Clear sight-tube plumbed to two bulkhead fittings (top + bottom) on the drum and/or settler; UV-shielded. Improved-edition addition; absent in as-built.
parts.function: Lets you see the liquid level AND the oil/water interface from outside a sealed opaque drum — so you can set port elevations and skim only when the layer is thick enough.
parts.spec: Clear PVC/poly sight-tube, 2 fittings (top and bottom), UV-shielded to prevent yellowing/embrittlement. $15-25. Reads level and the oil/water interface height.
parts.howItWorks: A transparent tube tapped into the drum top and bottom follows the internal liquid level by simple hydrostatics; because oil and water have different colors/densities, the interface shows as a visible line in the tube. You watch the ~1/8-in oil band build before deciding to skim.
parts.asBuilt: None. The as-built drum is opaque with no way to see inside — port elevations were guessed and skim timing was blind.
parts.improved: A UV-shielded clear sight-tube on the drum (and clear sides on the 15-gal settler) so elevations are set empirically and the operator skims only when the interface says the oil layer is worth taking.
parts.source: Clear vinyl/PVC tubing + two bulkhead fittings; standard tank sight-gauge hardware.
parts.failureMode: Unshielded clear plastic yellows and embrittles under pond-side UV; a clogged tap gives a false reading; algae growth inside the tube obscures the interface over time.
parts.exploreNote: It turns a blind opaque drum into something you can read like a thermometer — you literally watch the eighth-inch of wax accumulate and skim only when it's ready.

parts.label: vent
parts.name: Gooseneck vent + screen
parts.realPart: Gooseneck (inverted-U) vent fitting with insect/debris screen, one on the drum and one on the settling vessel. Improved-edition addition.
parts.function: Keeps every vessel vented to atmosphere — pressure-neutral — while keeping rain, bugs, and debris out.
parts.spec: 2x gooseneck vents with screens; $8-12 for the pair. Mandatory safety item: the drum and settler are lidded and vented, NEVER sealed against pressure.
parts.howItWorks: The inverted-U shape lets displaced air (and any decomposition CO2 from the algae) escape as the level rises and fall, while the downward-facing screened mouth blocks rain and insects. Because the vessels are open to atmosphere, the cavitation loop can't build dangerous pressure in a tank that isn't rated for it.
parts.asBuilt: Not explicitly drawn as a discrete part, but the safety principle (vessels vented, never sealed) is stated throughout — the as-built relies on the open-head lid not being airtight.
parts.improved: Explicit gooseneck + screen on both the drum and the settling vessel, called out as a hard safety rule alongside the CO2/vent-path requirement.
parts.source: Marine/RV tank vents or shop-bent PVC gooseneck + stainless screen.
parts.failureMode: Screen clogs with algae/debris and the vent chokes; if someone seals a vessel 'to keep water out,' a blocked nozzle or gas buildup can over-pressure an unrated poly tank.
parts.exploreNote: The one part whose entire job is to make sure the tanks are never sealed — because a pressurized 55-gal poly drum is a rupture waiting to happen.

parts.label: storage
parts.name: Final storage — bladder OR jerricans
parts.realPart: As-built: collapsible hydrocarbon-compatible bladder (ATL/marine). Improved: spec'd hydrocarbon-rated TPU bladder (15-25 gal) OR 2x 6.5-gal HDPE jerricans + quick-connect tap.
parts.function: Holds the recovered waxy lipid product on deck until it's off-loaded ashore for candle rendering.
parts.spec: Bladder: capacity/material/ports all UNKNOWN in as-built [MEASURE]; must be hydrocarbon-compatible for a waxy product. Improved: TPU bladder 15-25 gal ($350-600) OR 2x 6.5-gal HDPE jerricans + tap ($60-100).
parts.howItWorks: The transfer pump moves skimmed/coalesced product into the storage vessel. A bladder collapses as it empties (no sloshing air space, flexible deck footprint); jerricans are cheap, rigid, and inert. Product is tapped off ashore.
parts.asBuilt: A collapsible bladder is listed as the fluid product tank AND the storage tank (shared part), but capacity, material, hydrocarbon compatibility, and port sizes are ALL unspecified — the single most under-defined part in the subsystem.
parts.improved: Kill the UNKNOWN: either a properly hydrocarbon-rated TPU bladder or — the cheap inert default — two 6.5-gal HDPE jerricans with a quick-connect off-load tap.
parts.source: ATL/marine fuel bladders; hydrocarbon-rated TPU bladders; standard HDPE jerricans (jerrican route is the recommended cheap default).
parts.failureMode: A plain water bladder used for a lipid product swells, leaches, or fails; an undersized/over-sloshing bladder shifts raft trim; bladder cost swings 10x ($60-600), the biggest single cost uncertainty in the whole demonstrator.
parts.exploreNote: This was the most hand-wavy part in the original design — 'a bladder,' full stop, with no size or material — and the improved fix is almost comically down-to-earth: two plastic gas cans.

parts.label: xferpump
parts.name: Transfer / off-load diaphragm pump
parts.realPart: 12V diaphragm/RV pump (Shurflo 4008 / SEAFLO 33 class), ~45-55 psi, hydrocarbon-compatible (Santoprene/Viton) wetted parts. Shared with Fluid subsystem.
parts.function: Moves skimmed product from drum -> settler -> final storage, and off-loads ashore. Transfer only — never the high-pressure nozzle feed.
parts.spec: 12V diaphragm, ~45-55 psi; self-priming; wetted parts must be hydrocarbon-compatible (Santoprene/Viton) for the waxy product. Draws through an inline suction strainer.
parts.howItWorks: A diaphragm pump flexes a membrane to draw and expel fluid through check valves — it self-primes and can move thick, semi-solid, or lumpy wax that a centrifugal bilge pump would stall on. It handles all the low-pressure transfer legs on isolating ball valves.
parts.asBuilt: The same diaphragm/RV pump handles both off-load and decant (shared part). Explicitly warned to keep it STRICTLY off the high-pressure loop — it can't cavitate and will be damaged if plumbed to the nozzle.
parts.improved: Same pump, but spec hydrocarbon-compatible Santoprene/Viton wetted parts and add an inline suction strainer; plumbed skimmer -> pump -> coalescer -> storage with ball valves isolating each leg.
parts.source: Shurflo, SEAFLO, or generic 12V RV/marine diaphragm pumps.
parts.failureMode: A centrifugal bilge pump substituted here won't self-prime or move semi-solid wax. Non-hydrocarbon diaphragm/valves swell and fail on the lipid product. Plumbed to the HP loop by mistake, it's destroyed.
parts.exploreNote: It has to move a product that's halfway between oil and candle wax — semi-solid — which is exactly why it's a self-priming diaphragm pump and not the obvious cheap bilge pump.

parts.label: strainer
parts.name: Inline suction strainer
parts.realPart: Inline suction strainer on the transfer-pump inlet. Improved-edition addition.
parts.function: Keeps wax lumps and debris out of the transfer pump so its check valves don't jam.
parts.spec: Inline suction strainer, $10-20; sized to protect the diaphragm pump inlet without starving it. Distinct from the fine mesh/basket strainers in the Fluid subsystem (those protect the nozzle).
parts.howItWorks: A simple screened basket in the suction line traps congealed wax chunks and debris before they reach the diaphragm pump's check valves — the failure point that would otherwise stick open and kill priming.
parts.asBuilt: Not present as a distinct part; the as-built transfer pump draws unprotected.
parts.improved: Added on the transfer-pump suction as cheap insurance for the pump handling a lumpy, semi-solid product.
parts.source: Marine/irrigation inline strainers.
parts.failureMode: Screen clogs with wax and starves the pump (loss of prime); too fine a mesh restricts the thick product flow.
parts.exploreNote: A two-dollar-job part that exists purely because the 'oil' being pumped is really congealing wax that loves to jam a pump's valves.

parts.label: float
parts.name: Level / float switch
parts.realPart: 12V float switch controlling drum fill level for displacement decanting.
parts.function: Tells the system when the drum level is high enough to spill oil over the weir and when to off-load — automates the displacement-decant timing.
parts.spec: 12V marine float switch, $15-25. Gates fill level for displacement decant / off-load.
parts.howItWorks: A float rides the liquid level and closes a switch at a set height. As fresh slurry raises the level to that point, the switch signals that the floating layer is being pushed over the weir — coordinating the 'raise level -> decant oil' cycle without constant human watching.
parts.asBuilt: Listed as controlling fill level for displacement decant — the automation link between rising level and oil spill.
parts.improved: Superseded in spirit by the MPPT load output + sight-glass approach for timing, but a float/level switch remains a valid low-cost level control; the improved separation gates skimming to calm windows rather than pure level.
parts.source: Any marine/bilge float switch supplier.
parts.failureMode: Float fouls with algae/wax and sticks, either never triggering or chattering; on a moving raft, wave motion can trip it falsely.
parts.exploreNote: It's the same dumb float switch as in a bilge pump — repurposed not to keep the boat from sinking, but to decide when to spill the wax.

parts.label: wax
parts.name: Byproduct (wax) handling — the recovered product
parts.realPart: The recovered material itself: a waxy lipid residue (NOT diesel, NOT HVO). Candle rendering is a shore-side after-step; no melting/molding gear on the raft.
parts.function: The subsystem's tangible output — a small floating wax/lipid fraction skimmed per batch, stored, and later rendered into candles ashore.
parts.spec: Waxy lipid residue; ~1/8-in floating layer per batch (reference jar: ~1/8 in oil over ~3-5/8 in green liquid). Yield-per-loop UNPROVEN [MEASURE at §7.6/§9.4]. HTL-type bio-crude/paraffin at best — no catalyst or hydrogen feed on board.
parts.howItWorks: Each cavitation pass lyses algae cells and cracks a few percent of organics into a light fraction that floats. Skimmed, buffered, coalesced, and stored, it's melted, water-separated, and poured into candle molds on shore. It is an under-indexed bonus — the honest lead value is cleaner water, not the wax.
parts.asBuilt: Framed as a candle-grade wax bonus; the raft carries no rendering gear. Explicitly NOT diesel/fuel and with NO verified throughput — 'experimental until independently tested.'
parts.improved: Same honest framing, hardened: hydrocarbon-rated storage, a coalescer to actually recover it cleanly, and permanent instrumentation to weigh grams-of-wax-out vs watt-hours-in on every run instead of asserting a yield.
parts.cost: $0 (it is the product) — rendering gear is a separate shore-side cost
parts.source: Produced by the machine; candle molds/wax-melting are ordinary craft-supply items, ashore.
parts.failureMode: The core unproven claim: yield/rate on a solar power budget may be too small to matter, and cavitation can emulsify the very oil you want. Overclaiming it as 'fuel' or quoting gal/day is the venture's honesty/liability firewall being breached.
parts.exploreNote: The whole 'algae-to-diesel robot' legend comes down to this: an eighth-inch of candle-grade wax per batch, unproven in rate — sold honestly as a bonus, not a fuel.
